topic: compiler autotuning; GPU code generation; energy-performance tradeoffs
status: bounded full-text finding from one sampled compiler framework study
claim: Large reported gains from automatic CPU/GPU code transformation should be interpreted within the tested benchmark, hardware, energy-meter boundary, and variant-search budget; those measurements do not establish expected gains on other workloads or platforms.
positive_evidence: OMP2HMPP reports 31x average speedup and 5.86x operations-per-watt improvement over its original OpenMP baseline on a PolyBench subset.
The experiment uses one blade with two Intel Westmere quad-core CPUs and two Nvidia Tesla M2050 GPUs; reported energy excludes chassis components outside that blade.
The paper states generated variants can grow exponentially with OpenMP blocks and caps configurations at 21 per simple block, identifying search pruning as future work.
counterevidence: The paper compares generated code against both OpenMP and hand-coded GPU versions and reports that some generated variants approach expert-written code, so the benchmark does demonstrate feasibility in its tested setup.
A small fixed testbed is sufficient to establish proof of capability on those kernels; it is only a limit on generalization, not a refutation.

sources.sections: Abstract; variant generation limitation; PolyBench evaluation, hardware and energy boundary; conclusion

falsifiable_test: On preregistered held-out kernels and full applications, compare generated OpenMP/HMPP variants with optimized CPU and hand-written GPU baselines on multiple GPU generations. Fix compiler/search budgets, include compilation time, report the complete runtime-energy Pareto frontier, and define meter boundary. The boundedness concern weakens if gains persist across workloads/platforms within a practical fixed search cost.
limitations: One paper, a selected PolyBench subset and one historical hardware blade; no current hardware, independent replication, or full applications were audited.

status: bounded synthesis from one sampled platform proposal and proof-of-concept
claim: Publishing workflows and a shared systems-ML scoreboard may make artifacts more inspectable, but infrastructure presence alone does not establish that independent teams reproduce results faster, reduce variance, or obtain stable rankings across platforms.
positive_evidence: ReQuEST proposes standardized portable workflows, artifact evaluation, quality/efficiency Pareto reporting and an open tournament model.
The paper includes a proof-of-concept live scoreboard spanning models, frameworks, datasets and volunteer mobile devices.
counterevidence: The live-scoreboard demonstration shows that collaborative benchmarking infrastructure is technically feasible and can expose cross-stack variation.
The paper is primarily a platform proposal and does not claim a randomized evaluation of reproduction outcomes; the proposed metrics are an extension, not a contradiction.

sources.sections: Abstract; platform and artifact-evaluation design; live scoreboard proof of concept; future work

falsifiable_test: Randomly assign blinded reproduction teams to a standardized tournament workflow or conventional paper artifact package on matched systems-ML tasks. Measure artifact execution success, time-to-reproduction, result variance and ranking stability under a preregistered set of hardware/workload changes. The claim weakens if workflow assignment does not improve these outcomes.
limitations: Single platform proposal and an early proof of concept; this audit does not establish later ReQuEST adoption or evaluate subsequent tournaments.

topic: programming-language semantics; lambda calculus; complexity theory
status: bounded interpretation of one peer-reviewed formal result
claim: The audited invariance theorem establishes asymptotic time/space reasonability for deterministic weak call-by-value λ-calculus under its stated cost measures and Boolean-output assumptions; it does not by itself identify a canonical practical implementation or cover unrestricted evaluation strategies.
positive_evidence: The theorem proves polynomial-time and constant-factor-space simulation between Turing machines and the specified weak call-by-value calculus for Boolean-valued functions, when time and space are in Ω(n).
The paper formalizes core results in Coq and explicitly describes the result as resolving the stated problem for this fragment.
counterevidence: The paper itself notes that weak call-by-value is a relevant eager-functional model and is already Turing-complete, giving the theorem meaningful scope beyond a purely toy calculus.
A mechanized proof strengthens confidence in the formal claims; the limitation concerns inference to implementations or other strategies, not the theorem under its assumptions.

sources.sections: Abstract; Theorem 2; Sections 2–6; Coq formalization and implementation caveat

falsifiable_test: Implement the proof’s simulation and compare it with alternative verified weak-CbV machines on a preregistered finite program suite, measuring constants in time and peak space while checking model assumptions. Test other evaluation strategies only with separate formal proofs; an implementation benchmark cannot refute the asymptotic theorem but can test practical overhead claims.
limitations: One formal paper, a specific deterministic evaluation strategy, natural β-step/maximum-term-size measures and Boolean-valued functions; asymptotic theorem does not offer universal finite-input constants or cover full λ-calculus.
